result:
I'd make it painless to admit you were wrong.

Not "make people smarter" or "end war," though I'd take those too. But when I look at how things go badly, a surprising amount of it traces back to one moment: someone realizes, or half-realizes, that they were mistaken, and the cost of saying so feels unbearable. Admitting it means losing face, status, identity, the respect of their group, the story they've told about themselves for twenty years. So they dig in. Then they defend the digging. Then other people defend them. Whole institutions calcify around errors nobody can afford to name.

If changing your mind felt like relief, like setting down something heavy, instead of like a small death, I think a lot would follow. Arguments would become collaborative instead of combative. People could say "I don't know" without flinching. Apologies would come faster and mean more. Science would move quicker, politics would be less tribal, and families would carry fewer decades-long grudges built on something someone said once and couldn't take back.

Part of why this appeals to me personally is that I'm wrong fairly often, and the best version of me is the one that can say "oh, you're right, I missed that" without any need to save face. I'd want that ease for everyone.

What about you? I'm curious what made you ask.
